entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6694"/><div sID="gen10254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6694"/>6-9. These verses rather describe the wonders of the flood than the creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.7.19">Ge 7:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5">2Pe 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.6">6</reference>). God's method of arresting the flood and making its waters subside is poetically called a "rebuke" (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Is 50:2</reference>), and the process of the flood's subsiding by undulations among the hills and valleys is vividly described. <div eID="gen10254" type="x-p"/>

In rain and dew from His chambers (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>), and fountains and streams, they give drink to thirsting animals and fertilize the soil. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6701"/><div sID="gen10264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6701"/>27-30. The entire dependence of this immense family on God is set forth. With Him, to kill or make alive is equally easy. To hide His face is to withdraw favor (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.1">Psa 13:1</reference>). By His spirit, or breath, or mere word, He gives life. It is His constant providence which repairs the wastes of time and disease. <div eID="gen10264" type="x-p"/>
